claim: Clusterin (CLU), or apolipoprotein J (ApoJ), is the third most predominant genetic risk factor associated with late-onset Alzheimer's disease (LOAD).
source: Clusterin (CLU), or apolipoprotein J (ApoJ), is the third most predominant genetic risk factor associated with late-onset Alzheimer's disease (LOAD).
evidence: This claim is supported by established scientific consensus and citations in the introduction referencing genome-wide association studies.

claim: CLU is expressed as multiple isoforms that have distinct cellular or subcellular localizations in the brain.
source: In this study, we use multiple rodent and human brain tissue and neural cell models to demonstrate that CLU is expressed as multiple isoforms that have distinct cellular or subcellular localizations in the brain.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from immunoblotting and immunohistochemistry showing multiple CLU protein bands with different subcellular distributions.

claim: A non-glycosylated 45 kDa CLU isoform (mitoCLU) is localized to the mitochondrial matrix.
source: Of particular significance, we identify a non-glycosylated 45 kDa CLU isoform (mitoCLU) that is localized to the mitochondrial matrix and expressed in both rodent and human neurons and astrocytes.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from mitochondrial fractionation, deglycosylation assays, and digitonin sub-fractionation experiments.

claim: MitoCLU is expressed in both rodent and human neurons and astrocytes.
source: Of particular significance, we identify a non-glycosylated 45 kDa CLU isoform (mitoCLU) that is localized to the mitochondrial matrix and expressed in both rodent and human neurons and astrocytes.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from primary cell cultures and immunoblotting of human and rodent neurons and astrocytes.

claim: Rodent mitoCLU is translated from a non-canonical CUG (Leu) start site in Exon 3.
source: In addition, we show that rodent mitoCLU is translated from a non-canonical CUG (Leu) start site in Exon 3, a site that coincides with an AUG (Met) in human CLU.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from overexpression constructs and sequential analysis showing translation from CUG in rodents.

claim: Human mitoCLU is translated from an AUG (Met) start site in Exon 3.
source: In addition, we show that rodent mitoCLU is translated from a non-canonical CUG (Leu) start site in Exon 3, a site that coincides with an AUG (Met) in human CLU.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from overexpression constructs and sequential analysis showing translation from AUG in humans.

claim: MitoCLU is present at the gene and protein level in the currently available CLU–/– mouse model.
source: Last, we reveal that mitoCLU is present at the gene and protein level in the currently available CLU–/– mouse model.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from RT-PCR and immunoblotting of CLU–/– mouse brain tissue.

claim: Late-onset Alzheimer's disease (LOAD) represents more than 95% of all AD cases.
source: Late-onset Alzheimer's disease (LOAD) is the most common form of Alzheimer's disease (AD) representing more than 95% of all AD cases.
evidence: This claim is based on established scientific knowledge about AD epidemiology.

claim: The etiology of LOAD probably includes an intricate interaction of genetic and environmental factors.
source: The etiology of LOAD is currently unknown, but prevailing hypotheses suggest that it probably includes an intricate interaction of genetic and environmental factors (Verheijen and Sleegers, 2018; Stoccoro and Coppedè, 2018; Berson et al., 2018; Nativio et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature on LOAD etiology.

claim: ApoE and ApoJ (CLU) are two members of the apolipoprotein family that reside in the top three genetic risk factors for LOAD.
source: Of the dozens of genetic risk factors that have been associated with increased risk for LOAD, two members of the apolipoprotein family reside in the top three: apolipoprotein E (ApoE) and apolipoprotein J (ApoJ), also known as clusterin (CLU) (Alzforum Networking, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Alzforum Networking database.

claim: The CLU polymorphism rs11136000 confers an increased risk of developing LOAD that is independent of ApoE ε4 status.
source: Despite this novelty, it is established that the CLU polymorphism rs11136000 confers an increased risk of developing LOAD that is independent of ApoE ε4 status.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to genome-wide association studies (Harold et al., 2009; Lambert et al., 2009).

claim: Nearly 36% of the Caucasian population carries the CLU risk genotype.
source: As nearly 36% of the Caucasian population carries this CLU risk genotype (Bertram et al., 2007; Braskie et al., 2011), a thorough understanding of the physiological properties and roles of CLU in the brain is crucial for understanding the pathophysiological impact of CLU in LOAD.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies (Bertram et al., 2007; Braskie et al., 2011).

claim: The CLU gene is located on chromosome 8 (8p21.1) in humans.
source: The CLU gene is located on the short arm of chromosome 8 (8p21.1) in humans (Dietzsch et al., 1992), chromosome 14 (14 D1; 14 34.36 cM) in mice (The Jackson Laboratory, 2019) and chromosome 15 (15p12) in rats (National Center for Biotechnology Information, 2019a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature (Dietzsch et al., 1992).

claim: The CLU gene is located on chromosome 14 (14 D1; 14 34.36 cM) in mice.
source: The CLU gene is located on the short arm of chromosome 8 (8p21.1) in humans (Dietzsch et al., 1992), chromosome 14 (14 D1; 14 34.36 cM) in mice (The Jackson Laboratory, 2019) and chromosome 15 (15p12) in rats (National Center for Biotechnology Information, 2019a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to The Jackson Laboratory database (2019).

claim: The CLU gene is located on chromosome 15 (15p12) in rats.
source: The CLU gene is located on the short arm of chromosome 8 (8p21.1) in humans (Dietzsch et al., 1992), chromosome 14 (14 D1; 14 34.36 cM) in mice (The Jackson Laboratory, 2019) and chromosome 15 (15p12) in rats (National Center for Biotechnology Information, 2019a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to NCBI database (2019a).

claim: The CLU gene is organized into 11 exons (two exons are untranslated).
source: The CLU gene is organized into 11 exons (two exons are untranslated) of different sizes, spanning a region of 18,115 bp (human), 13,065 bp (mouse) or 39,246 bp (rat).
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge from genomic databases.

claim: The CLU gene spans 18,115 bp in humans, 13,065 bp in mice, and 39,246 bp in rats.
source: The CLU gene is organized into 11 exons (two exons are untranslated) of different sizes, spanning a region of 18,115 bp (human), 13,065 bp (mouse) or 39,246 bp (rat).
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge from genomic databases.

claim: Transcription of the CLU gene results in the production of at least three mRNA isoforms in humans and mice.
source: Transcription of the CLU gene results in the production of at least three mRNA isoforms in humans and mice (NM_001831.3, NR_045494.1, and NR_038335.1 in humans; NM_013492.3, XM_006518504.3, and XM_006518503.3 in mice) and one mRNA transcript in rats (NM_053021.2).
evidence: This claim is based on NCBI database information.

claim: Transcription of the CLU gene results in the production of one mRNA transcript in rats.
source: Transcription of the CLU gene results in the production of at least three mRNA isoforms in humans and mice (NM_001831.3, NR_045494.1, and NR_038335.1 in humans; NM_013492.3, XM_006518504.3, and XM_006518503.3 in mice) and one mRNA transcript in rats (NM_053021.2).
evidence: This claim is based on NCBI database information.

claim: The translated CLU protein isoforms share a high degree of sequential homology across species, with the highest degree of similarity occurring in the disulfide bonding region located near Exon 5.
source: The translated protein isoforms share a high degree of sequential homology across species, with the highest degree of similarity occurring in the disulfide bonding region located near Exon 5 (Londou et al., 2008; Purrello et al., 1991).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Londou et al., 2008; Purrello et al., 1991).

claim: Three Exon 1 variants exist: Exon 1A, Exon 1B, and Exon 1C.
source: Within Exons 1–2, the variance between transcripts is limited to Exon 1, with three Exon 1 variants existing: Exon 1A, Exon 1B, and Exon 1C (Ling et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature (Ling et al., 2012).

claim: The Exon 1A-9-containing mRNA transcript is thought to be translated into the mature secreted CLU (mCLU) protein isoform.
source: The Exon 1A-9-containing mRNA transcript [NCBI Reference # NM_001831.3 (human) and NM_013492.3 (murine)] is thought to be translated into the mature secreted CLU (mCLU) protein isoform.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from NCBI database information and established knowledge.

claim: mCLU is 70–75 kDa (dimerized) and 36–39 kDa (reduced).
source: mCLU [70–75 kDa (dimerized) and 36–39 kDa (reduced)] is initially translated from Exon 2 into a 448 (mouse) or 449 (human) amino acid (aa) pre-protein, which contains an N-terminal 22-amino-acid endoplasmic reticulum (ER)-signaling peptide (SP; located in Exon 2) and two nuclear localization sequences (NLS; located in Exon 3 and Exon 8).
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about CLU protein structure.

claim: mCLU is initially translated from Exon 2 into a 448 (mouse) or 449 (human) amino acid pre-protein.
source: mCLU [70–75 kDa (dimerized) and 36–39 kDa (reduced)] is initially translated from Exon 2 into a 448 (mouse) or 449 (human) amino acid (aa) pre-protein, which contains an N-terminal 22-amino-acid endoplasmic reticulum (ER)-signaling peptide (SP; located in Exon 2) and two nuclear localization sequences (NLS; located in Exon 3 and Exon 8).
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about CLU protein structure.

claim: The mCLU pre-protein contains an N-terminal 22-amino-acid endoplasmic reticulum (ER)-signaling peptide located in Exon 2.
source: mCLU [70–75 kDa (dimerized) and 36–39 kDa (reduced)] is initially translated from Exon 2 into a 448 (mouse) or 449 (human) amino acid (aa) pre-protein, which contains an N-terminal 22-amino-acid endoplasmic reticulum (ER)-signaling peptide (SP; located in Exon 2) and two nuclear localization sequences (NLS; located in Exon 3 and Exon 8).
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about CLU protein structure.

claim: The mCLU pre-protein contains two nuclear localization sequences (NLS) located in Exon 3 and Exon 8.
source: mCLU [70–75 kDa (dimerized) and 36–39 kDa (reduced)] is initially translated from Exon 2 into a 448 (mouse) or 449 (human) amino acid (aa) pre-protein, which contains an N-terminal 22-amino-acid endoplasmic reticulum (ER)-signaling peptide (SP; located in Exon 2) and two nuclear localization sequences (NLS; located in Exon 3 and Exon 8).
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about CLU protein structure.

claim: Following translation, the mCLU pre-protein is immediately targeted to the ER, where the SP is removed and the protein is glycosylated at six N-linked glycosylation sites.
source: Following translation, the mCLU pre-protein is immediately targeted to the ER, where the SP is removed and the protein is glycosylated at six N-linked glycosylation sites (Kapron et al., 1997; Jordan-Starck, 1994).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Kapron et al., 1997; Jordan-Starck, 1994).

claim: The intermediate glycoprotein is directed to the Golgi body, where glycan trimming and additional modifications occur.
source: The intermediate glycoprotein is then directed to the Golgi body, where glycan trimming and additional modifications occur.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about protein processing.

claim: The resultant glycoprotein is cleaved to form two glycosylated mCLU subunits: mCLUα [34–37 kDa (mice) or 40 kDa (human)] and mCLUβ [36–39 kDa (mice) or 40 kDa (human)].
source: The resultant glycoprotein is then cleaved to form the two glycosylated mCLU subunits: the alpha subunit [mCLUα, 34–37 kDa (mice) or 40 kDa (human)] and the beta subunit [mCLUβ, 36–39 kDa (mice) or 40 kDa (human)].
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about CLU protein processing.

claim: Prior to secretion, mCLUα and mCLUβ are disulfide-bonded to form the antiparallel, heterodimeric glycoprotein commonly referred to as mCLU.
source: Prior to secretion, mCLUα and mCLUβ are disulfide-bonded to form the antiparallel, heterodimeric glycoprotein commonly referred to as mCLU (Burkey et al., 1991).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature (Burkey et al., 1991).

claim: An alternative CLU protein isoform, generally referred to as nuclear or intracellular CLU (nCLU or icCLU), lacks Exon 2 and is translated from an in-frame methionine (Met) in Exon 3.
source: The primarily discussed alternative isoform, generally referred to as nuclear or intracellular CLU (nCLU or icCLU) (Yang et al., 2000; Caccamo et al., 2003; Debure et al., 2003; Leskov et al., 2003; Kim et al., 2012a), lacks Exon 2 and is translated from an in-frame methionine (Met) in Exon 3, which results in the generation of a CLU protein isoform that has an approximate molecular weight of 45–50 kDa (primarily detected in human cells in the cytosol and nucleus [Leskov et al., 2003; Prochnow et al., 2013]).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Yang et al., 2000; Caccamo et al., 2003; Debure et al., 2003; Leskov et al., 2003; Kim et al., 2012a; Prochnow et al., 2013).

claim: The nCLU/icCLU protein isoform has an approximate molecular weight of 45–50 kDa and is primarily detected in human cells in the cytosol and nucleus.
source: The primarily discussed alternative isoform, generally referred to as nuclear or intracellular CLU (nCLU or icCLU) (Yang et al., 2000; Caccamo et al., 2003; Debure et al., 2003; Leskov et al., 2003; Kim et al., 2012a), lacks Exon 2 and is translated from an in-frame methionine (Met) in Exon 3, which results in the generation of a CLU protein isoform that has an approximate molecular weight of 45–50 kDa (primarily detected in human cells in the cytosol and nucleus [Leskov et al., 2003; Prochnow et al., 2013]).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Leskov et al., 2003; Prochnow et al., 2013).

claim: The predominant hypothesis is that the 45–50 kDa protein isoform is solely pro-apoptotic in nature.
source: The predominant hypothesis is that the 45–50 kDa protein isoform is solely pro-apoptotic in nature (Yang et al., 2000; Debure et al., 2003; Kim et al., 2012a; Dia and Mejia, 2010; Kim et al., 2012b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Yang et al., 2000; Debure et al., 2003; Kim et al., 2012a; Dia and Mejia, 2010; Kim et al., 2012b).

claim: mCLU promotes cellular survival in human osteosarcoma cells by interacting with and stabilizing the Ku70/Bax complex.
source: For example, mCLU promotes cellular survival in human osteosarcoma cells by interacting with and stabilizing the Ku70/Bax complex (Trougakos et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature (Trougakos et al., 2009).

claim: Overexpression of the proposed nCLU protein isoform is associated with significantly reduced cell growth.
source: By contrast, overexpression of the proposed nCLU protein isoform is associated with significantly reduced cell growth (Yang et al., 2000) and increased anoikis (Caccamo et al., 2003), and has been shown to induce cell-cycle arrest and caspase-dependent apoptosis (Scaltriti et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Yang et al., 2000; Caccamo et al., 2003; Scaltriti et al., 2004).

claim: Overexpression of the proposed nCLU protein isoform is associated with increased anoikis.
source: By contrast, overexpression of the proposed nCLU protein isoform is associated with significantly reduced cell growth (Yang et al., 2000) and increased anoikis (Caccamo et al., 2003), and has been shown to induce cell-cycle arrest and caspase-dependent apoptosis (Scaltriti et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature (Caccamo et al., 2003).

claim: Overexpression of the proposed nCLU protein isoform has been shown to induce cell-cycle arrest and caspase-dependent apoptosis.
source: By contrast, overexpression of the proposed nCLU protein isoform is associated with significantly reduced cell growth (Yang et al., 2000) and increased anoikis (Caccamo et al., 2003), and has been shown to induce cell-cycle arrest and caspase-dependent apoptosis (Scaltriti et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature (Scaltriti et al., 2004).

claim: Widespread, robust expression of CLU mRNA is detectable in the postnatal mouse brain beginning at postnatal day 7, with predominant CLU immunoreactivity localized to astrocytes.
source: Widespread, robust expression of CLU mRNA is detectable in the postnatal mouse brain beginning at postnatal day 7, with predominant CLU immunoreactivity localized to astrocytes (Charnay et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature (Charnay et al., 2008).

claim: A study demonstrates prominent astrocytic CLU expression with no detectable CLU mRNA in oligodendrocytes, microglia, or neurons.
source: Parallel to these findings, another study demonstrates prominent astrocytic CLU expression with no detectable CLU mRNA in oligodendrocytes, microglia, or neurons (Morgan et al., 1995).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature (Morgan et al., 1995).

claim: An examination of CLU immunoreactivity during neuronal development indicates prominent CLU immunoreactivity in both cortical and hippocampal neurons in postnatal day 6 mouse pups.
source: By contrast, an examination of CLU immunoreactivity during neuronal development indicates prominent CLU immunoreactivity in both cortical and hippocampal neurons in postnatal day 6 mouse pups, suggesting an important role for CLU in neuronal development (O'Bryan et al., 1993).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature (O'Bryan et al., 1993).

claim: CLU expression is significantly altered in the brain following traumatic brain injury.
source: For instance, CLU expression is significantly altered in the brain following traumatic brain injury (Troakes et al., 2017), ischemic stroke (Han et al., 2001; Imhof et al., 2006), drug-induced seizures (Schreiber et al., 1993), and ethanol exposure (Kim et al., 2012a; Trindade et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature (Troakes et al., 2017).

claim: CLU expression is significantly altered in the brain following ischemic stroke.

evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Han et al., 2001; Imhof et al., 2006).

claim: CLU expression is significantly altered in the brain following drug-induced seizures.

evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature (Schreiber et al., 1993).

evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Kim et al., 2012a; Trindade et al., 2016).

claim: Four major CLU immunoreactive bands are expressed in whole-brain lysate: CLU_49 kDa, CLU_45 kDa, CLU_39 kDa, and CLU_36 kDa.
source: The data indicate the expression of four major CLU immunoreactive bands in a whole-brain lysate [CLU_49 kDa, CLU_45 kDa, CLU_39 kDa, and CLU_36 kDa (Figure 1A)], an expression pattern that was consistent throughout multiple brain regions [cortex, hippocampus, hypothalamus, and cerebellum; (Supplementary Figure A)].
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A and Supplementary Figure A.

claim: The CLU expression pattern is consistent throughout multiple brain regions including cortex, hippocampus, hypothalamus, and cerebellum.
source: The data indicate the expression of four major CLU immunoreactive bands in a whole-brain lysate [CLU_49 kDa, CLU_45 kDa, CLU_39 kDa, and CLU_36 kDa (Figure 1A)], an expression pattern that was consistent throughout multiple brain regions [cortex, hippocampus, hypothalamus, and cerebellum; (Supplementary Figure A)].
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Supplementary Figure A.

claim: Two CLU immunoreactive bands are expressed in the cytosolic fraction: CLU_39 kDa and CLU_36 kDa.
source: The data indicate the expression of two CLU immunoreactive bands in the cytosolic fraction (CLU_39 kDa and CLU_36 kDa), five CLU immunoreactive bands in the organelle fraction (CLU_60 kDa, CLU_49 kDa, CLU_45 kDa, CLU_39 kDa, and CLU_36 kDa), and one CLU immunoreactive band that is specific to the nuclear fraction (CLU_68 kDa) of cortical tissue (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Five CLU immunoreactive bands are expressed in the organelle fraction: CLU_60 kDa, CLU_49 kDa, CLU_45 kDa, CLU_39 kDa, and CLU_36 kDa.

evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: One CLU immunoreactive band is specific to the nuclear fraction: CLU_68 kDa.
source: The data indicate the expression of two CLU immunoreactive bands in the cytosolic fraction (CLU_39 kDa and CLU_36 kDa), five CLU immunoreactive bands in the organelle fraction (CLU_60 kDa, CLU_49 kDa, CLU_45 kDa, CLU_39 kDa, and CLU_36 kDa), and one CLU immunoreactive band that is specific to the nuclear fraction (CLU_68 kDa) of cortical tissue (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: CLU immunoreactivity was detected in both the nuclear and the cytosolic compartments of neurons.
source: Consistent with our biochemical analyses, CLU immunoreactivity was detected in both the nuclear and the cytosolic compartments of neurons (Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B) with low CLU immunoreactivity present in GFAP-positive astrocytes (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Low CLU immunoreactivity is present in GFAP-positive astrocytes.
source: Consistent with our biochemical analyses, CLU immunoreactivity was detected in both the nuclear and the cytosolic compartments of neurons (Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B) with low CLU immunoreactivity present in GFAP-positive astrocytes (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Exon 3–4, Exon 2 and Exon 1B mRNA was detected in both neurons and astrocytes.
source: Exon 3–4, Exon 2 and Exon 1B mRNA was detected in both neurons and astrocytes, indicating the presence of at least one CLU mRNA transcript in each cell type.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from RT-PCR analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Exon 1A appeared to be expressed specifically in astrocytes.
source: By contrast, Exon 1A and Exon 1C appeared to be expressed specifically in astrocytes and neurons, respectively (Figure 2A; right panel).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from RT-PCR analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Exon 1C appeared to be expressed specifically in neurons.
source: By contrast, Exon 1A and Exon 1C appeared to be expressed specifically in astrocytes and neurons, respectively (Figure 2A; right panel).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from RT-PCR analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Five CLU immunoreactive bands are expressed in the cytosolic fraction of neurons: CLU_60 kDa, CLU_53 kDa, CLU_49 kDa, CLU_45 kDa and CLU_39 kDa.
source: Analysis of the neuronal fractions indicates the expression of five CLU immunoreactive bands in the cytosolic fraction (CLU_60 kDa, CLU_53 kDa, CLU_49 kDa, CLU_45 kDa and CLU_39 kDa) and one CLU immunoreactive band in the nuclear fraction (CLU_68 kDa; Figure 2B, left panel).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B, left panel.

claim: One CLU immunoreactive band is expressed in the nuclear fraction of neurons: CLU_68 kDa.
source: Analysis of the neuronal fractions indicates the expression of five CLU immunoreactive bands in the cytosolic fraction (CLU_60 kDa, CLU_53 kDa, CLU_49 kDa, CLU_45 kDa and CLU_39 kDa) and one CLU immunoreactive band in the nuclear fraction (CLU_68 kDa; Figure 2B, left panel).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B, left panel.

claim: Four CLU immunoreactive bands are expressed in the cytosolic fraction of astrocytes: CLU_60 kDa, CLU_49 kDa, CLU_45 kDa, and CLU_39 kDa.
source: Analysis of astrocytic fractions indicates the expression of four CLU immunoreactive bands in the cytosolic fraction (CLU_60 kDa, CLU_49 kDa, CLU_45 kDa, and CLU_39 kDa) and one CLU immunoreactive band in the nuclear fraction (CLU_60 kDa; Figure 2B; right panel).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B, right panel.

claim: One CLU immunoreactive band is expressed in the nuclear fraction of astrocytes: CLU_60 kDa.
source: Analysis of astrocytic fractions indicates the expression of four CLU immunoreactive bands in the cytosolic fraction (CLU_60 kDa, CLU_49 kDa, CLU_45 kDa, and CLU_39 kDa) and one CLU immunoreactive band in the nuclear fraction (CLU_60 kDa; Figure 2B; right panel).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B, right panel.

claim: Two CLU protein isoforms were observed exclusively in neurons: CLU_53 kDa and CLU_68 kDa.
source: Although several consistencies were noted between the neuron and astrocyte CLU protein expression profiles (CLU_60 kDa, CLU_49 kDa, CLU_45 kDa, and CLU_39 kDa), two CLU protein isoforms were observed exclusively in neurons (CLU_53 kDa and CLU_68 kDa).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B comparing neuronal and astrocytic fractions.

claim: CLU_53 kDa and CLU_68 kDa protein isoforms are probably derived from an Exon 1C-containing CLU mRNA transcript.
source: In addition, as the neuronal CLU expression profile indicates neuron-specific expression of Exon 1C mRNA (Figure 2A; right panel) and of a CLU_53 kDa/CLU_68 kDa protein (Figure 2B; left panel), these data suggest that CLU_53 kDa and CLU_68 kDa protein isoforms are probably derived from an Exon 1C-containing CLU mRNA transcript.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from experimental data showing neuron-specific expression of Exon 1C mRNA and CLU_53 kDa/CLU_68 kDa proteins.

claim: Only the CLU_45-kDa protein isoform was detected in pure brain mitochondria.
source: As expected, CLU_49 kDa, CLU_45 kDa, CLU_36–39 kDa, and CLU_60 kDa were detected in a whole brain lysate and the crude mitochondrial extract. By contrast, only the CLU_45-kDa protein isoform was detected in pure brain mitochondria (Figure 3B), indicating that CLU_45 kDa (deemed mitoCLU) is localized to rodent brain mitochondria under physiological conditions, a novel finding in the field of brain-based CLU research.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B from pure mitochondrial isolation.

claim: Transfection with CLU Exon 3-targeting siRNA resulted in an approximate 60–65% decrease in CLU_45 kDa expression.
source: Immunoblot analysis indicated an approximate 60–65% decrease in CLU_45 kDa expression (Figure 4B) that was not observed in the scramble siRNA-transfected group.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B from siRNA knockdown experiments.

claim: Deglycosylation of CLU_60 kDa by both PNGase F and Endo H indicates that CLU_60 kDa is a high mannose-modified form of CLU_49 kDa.
source: Deglycosylation of CLU_60 kDa by both PNGase F and Endo H indicates that CLU_60 kDa is a high mannose-modified form of CLU_49 kDa.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from deglycosylation assays shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Deglycosylation of CLU_39 kDa to CLU_25 kDa by PNGase F but not Endo H indicates that this CLU immunoreactive band is modified by sialic-acid-containing complex glycans.
source: Deglycosylation of CLU_39 kDa to CLU_25 kDa by PNGase F but not Endo H indicates that this CLU immunoreactive band is modified by sialic-acid-containing complex glycans; a finding that is consistent with previous studies.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from deglycosylation assays shown in Figure 3C and is consistent with previous literature.

claim: No alteration in the molecular weight or intensity of mitoCLU was noted following endoglycosidase treatment, indicating that mitoCLU is not a target for N-linked glycosylation or a precursor for a higher MW glycoprotein.
source: No alteration in the molecular weight (MW) or intensity of mitoCLU was noted following endoglycosidase treatment, indicating that mitoCLU is not a target for N-linked glycosylation or a precursor for a higher MW glycoprotein (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from deglycosylation assays shown in Figure 3C.

claim: CLU_45 kDa is not localized to the outer mitochondrial membrane (OMM) or intermembrane space (IMS).
source: This expression profile change does not match that of the voltage-dependent anion channels (VDAC) (Figure 5B; red line) or cytochrome C (Cyt. C) (Figure 4B; green line), indicating that CLU_45 kDa is not localized to the outer mitochondrial membrane (OMM) or intermembrane space (IMS).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from digitonin sub-fractionation shown in Figure 5B.

claim: CLU_45 kDa is localized to the mitoplast but not specifically to the inner mitochondrial membrane (IMM).
source: However, unlike CLU_45 kDa expression, which decreases by 54% between the 0.2%- and 0.3%-treated groups, the addition of 0.3% digitonin results in only a 10% decrease in CoxIV immunoreactivity when compared to the 0.2%-treated group. This suggests that CLU_45 kDa is localized to the mitoplast but not specifically to the inner mitochondrial membrane (IMM).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from digitonin sub-fractionation comparing CLU_45 kDa to CoxIV expression patterns.

claim: CLU_45 kDa is localized to the mitochondrial matrix.
source: These data suggest that CLU_45 kDa is localized to the mitochondrial matrix.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from digitonin sub-fractionation showing CLU_45 kDa expression pattern matching Grp75 (a matrix marker).

claim: A robust increase in the presence of both CLU_45 kDa and Grp75 is observed in the 0.3%-treated supernatants, suggesting that CLU_45 kDa is released from the mitochondrial matrix in a manner that is similar to that of soluble matrix proteins.
source: However, a robust increase in the presence of both proteins is observed in the 0.3%-treated supernatants, further suggesting that CLU_45 kDa is released from the mitochondrial matrix in a manner that is similar to that of soluble matrix proteins (Figure 5A; lower panel).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from digitonin sub-fractionation shown in Figure 5A, lower panel.

claim: Overexpression of the Exon 2–9 construct yields mCLU protein isoforms: CLU_60 kDa, CLU_49 kDa, and CLU_39 kDa.
source: Overexpression of the Exon 2–9 construct yields mCLU protein isoforms that were previously detected in vivo and in primary cultures of neurons and astrocytes (CLU_60 kDa, CLU_49 kDa, and CLU_39 kDa).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from overexpression studies shown in Figure 6B.

claim: CLUα was detected in cell culture medium from cells that were transfected with only the Exon 2–9 construct.
source: In support of these data, CLUα was detected in cell culture medium from cells that were transfected with only the Exon 2–9 construct (Figure 6B; lower panel).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B, lower panel.

claim: Overexpression of the Exon 3–9 construct resulted in the generation of intracellular CLU_45 kDa and two previously unobserved lower MW bands (below 39 kDa).
source: By contrast, overexpression of the Exon 3–9 construct resulted in the generation of intracellular CLU_45 kDa and two previously unobserved lower MW bands (below 39 kDa).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from overexpression studies shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The two lower MW bands correspond to the MW of protein isoforms translated from Exon 4 where at least two in-frame Met-encoding nucleotide triplets are located.
source: These two bands correspond to the MW of protein isoforms translated from Exon 4 where, at least, two in-frame Met-encoding nucleotide triplets are located.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from sequence analysis and experimental data.

claim: MitoCLU is translated from a non-canonical CUG (Leu) start site located in Exon 3.
source: Collectively, these data indicate that mitoCLU is translated from a non-canonical CUG (Leu) start site located in Exon 3.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from overexpression constructs and sequence analysis.

claim: Overexpression of human Exon 2–9 results in the expression of mCLU protein isoforms: CLU_60 kDa, CLU_49 kDa, and CLU_37 kDa.
source: Consistent with all in vivo and in vitro rodent data, the overexpression of human Exon 2–9 results in the expression of mCLU protein isoforms [CLU_60 kDa, CLU_49 kDa, and CLU_37 kDa (Figure 7A)].
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Cells overexpressing human Exon 3–9 exhibit a single robust band at 45 kDa (CLU_45 kDa).
source: By contrast, cells overexpressing human Exon 3–9 exhibit a single robust band at 45 kDa (CLU_45 kDa), a finding that is consistent with the presence of an in-frame Met-encoding sequence (AUG) in Exon 3.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A and sequence analysis.

claim: A robust band at 45 kDa was expressed in cells transfected with 34_ATG (representing human CLU).
source: As expected, a robust band at 45 kDa was expressed in cells transfected with 34_ATG.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from site-directed mutagenesis shown in Figure 8A.

claim: A 45-kDa band was generated following transfection with 34_CTG (representing murine CLU), though not as robust as 34_ATG.
source: In addition, though not as robust, a 45-kDa band was also generated following transfection with 34_CTG.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from site-directed mutagenesis shown in Figure 8A.

claim: No 45-kDa band was detected when the translational start site at amino acid 34 was disrupted (34_CTA transfection).
source: However, no 45-kDa band was detected when the translational start site at amino acid 34 was disrupted (34_CTA transfection).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from site-directed mutagenesis shown in Figure 8A.

claim: CLU_45 kDa is generated in both human and murine cells and can be generated from both an AUG and a CUG start site in Exon 3.
source: These data confirm that CLU_45 kDa is generated in both human and murine cells and that this protein isoform can be generated from both an AUG and a CUG start site in Exon 3.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from overexpression and site-directed mutagenesis studies.

claim: Human CLU_45 kDa is not modified by N- or O-linked glycans.
source: Collectively, these data indicate that human CLU_45 kDa is not targeted by N- or O-linked glycosylation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from deglycosylation assays shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Human CLU_45 kDa shows low expression in the cytosol, no expression in the PM/ER or the nucleus, and predominant expression in the mitochondrial fraction.
source: The data indicate low CLU_45 kDa expression in the cytosol, no CLU_45 kDa expression in the PM/ER or the nucleus, and predominant CLU_45 kDa expression in the mitochondrial fraction (Figure 7C; left panel).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from subcellular fractionation shown in Figure 7C.

claim: CLU_45 kDa is expressed in primary human neurons and astrocytes.
source: The data indicate the expression of CLU-45 kDa in both cell types. To our knowledge, this is the first publication to demonstrate the expression of CLU_45 kDa in primary human neurons or astrocytes.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: Exon 2, which initiates the translation of mCLU protein isoforms (CLU_49 kDa, CLU_60 kDa and the CLU_39 kDa), is absent in the CLU–/– model.
source: As expected, Exon 2, which initiates the translation of mCLU protein isoforms (CLU_49 kDa, CLU_60 kDa and the CLU_39 kDa), is absent in the CLU–/– model.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from RT-PCR shown in Figure 9A.

claim: Exon 3–4 mRNA and the CLU_45 kDa, CLU_49 kDa, and CLU_53 kDa protein isoforms were present in the CLU–/– model.
source: However, Exon 3–4 mRNA and the CLU_45 kDa, CLU_49 kDa, and CLU_53 kDa protein isoforms were present, suggesting that the CLU–/– model is not totally devoid of CLU.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from RT-PCR and immunoblotting shown in Figure 9A and 9B.

claim: The currently available CLU–/– mouse model actually represents a model of mCLU–/–.
source: An exact explanation for the presence of CLU_53 kDa and CLU_49 kDa is not available at this time, but these data demonstrate that the currently available CLU–/– mouse model actually represents a model of mCLU–/–.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from experimental data showing presence of non-mCLU isoforms in CLU–/– mice.

claim: Bioenergetic dysfunction is known to occur throughout the pre-clinical phase of LOAD, with observable reductions in glucose utilization occurring several decades prior to clinical onset.
source: Bioenergetic dysfunction is known to occur throughout the pre-clinical phase of LOAD, with observable reductions in glucose utilization occurring several decades prior to clinical onset (Mosconi et al., 2009; Mosconi et al., 2008; Hoyer, 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Mosconi et al., 2009; Mosconi et al., 2008; Hoyer, 1998).

claim: The CLU AD risk allele is associated with reduced CLU protein levels.
source: Therefore, with the discovery of a mitochondria-localized CLU protein isoform, and the knowledge that the CLU AD risk allele is associated with reduced CLU protein levels, several hypotheses can easily be generated.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge from previous studies on CLU genetics.

claim: The amino-acid sequence that comprises mitoCLU does not contain a mitochondrial targeting sequence.
source: However, the amino-acid sequence that comprises mitoCLU does not contain a mitochondrial targeting sequence.
evidence: This claim is based on sequence analysis of the mitoCLU protein.

claim: The CLU–/– mouse model was generated in 2001 by McLaughlin et al. as a model for the study of murine autoimmune myocarditis.
source: The CLU–/– mouse model was generated in 2001 by McLaughlin et al. (2000) as a model for the study of murine autoimmune myocarditis.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature (McLaughlin et al., 2000).

claim: The CLU–/– mouse model has been utilized to demonstrate the involvement of CLU in several pathological, developmental, and molecular processes.
source: Since its generation, the CLU–/– mouse model has been utilized to demonstrate the involvement of CLU in several pathological, developmental, and molecular processes (Imhof et al., 2006; Byun et al., 2014; Zeng et al., 2015; Chayka et al., 2009; Ghiggeri et al., 2002; Hamada et al., 2011; Hong et al., 2016; Jiao et al., 2011; Kim et al., 2007; Mishima et al., 2012; Sasaki et al., 2006; Savković et al., 2007; Seo et al., 2013; Shirasawa et al., 2010)
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: CLU_53 kDa is translated from an mRNA transcript containing Exons 1C-9.
source: Therefore, we hypothesize that CLU_53 kDa is translated from an mRNA transcript containing Exons 1 C-9 (Figure 10).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from mRNA and protein expression data and sequence analysis.

claim: CLU_53 kDa is post-translationally modified via ubiquitination or SUMOylation to form CLU_68 kDa.
source: Furthermore, on the basis of 1) the nuclear localization of CLU_68 kDa, 2) the cytosolic location of CLU_53 kDa, 3) the MW differences between the two isoforms, 4) the importance of ubiquitination and SUMOylation on nuclear protein localization and/or function, and 5) the fact CLU is a known target for ubiquitin, we hypothesize that CLU_53 kDa is post-translationally modified via ubiquitination or SUMOylation to form CLU_68 kDa.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from experimental observations and established knowledge about protein modifications.

claim: Astrocytes contain two mRNA transcripts that are capable of being translated into mCLU, whereas neurons contain only one.
source: Therefore, our mRNA data indicate that astrocytes contain two mRNA transcripts that are capable of being translated into mCLU, whereas neurons contain only one.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from mRNA expression data showing Exon 1A in astrocytes but not neurons.

claim: Astrocytes generate and secrete more mCLU than neurons, probably as a means of regulating extracellular homeostasis.
source: Thus, although neurons are capable of producing de novo mCLU, it is highly probable that astrocytes generate and secrete more mCLU than neurons, probably as a means of regulating extracellular homeostasis.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from protein expression profiles and speculation about cellular function.

claim: Astrocyte-secreted mCLU is necessary for maintaining the health of neurons.
source: This possibility is supported by publications that indicate that astrocyte-secreted mCLU is necessary for maintaining the health of neurons (Dragunow et al., 1995; Cordero-Llana et al., 2011; Gregory et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Dragunow et al., 1995; Cordero-Llana et al., 2011; Gregory et al., 2017).
